functional_compartments.function_note: Classic example of a single named muscle whose index compartment is both anatomically distinct (separate muscle belly, per Gray's) and separately innervated (AIN/median vs ulnar for the rest).
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) (index portion of FDP typically has a separate muscle belly); von Schroeder HP, Botte MJ (1993) J Hand Surg -- FDP anatomic compartmentalization

motor_endplate_zones.method: modified Sihler's stain intramuscular nerve-dense region, with muscle-spindle abundance histology
motor_endplate_zones.notes: Supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, which 'mainly dominates the radial half'. About 7.20 cm2, the largest nerve-dense region measured in the study. Highest spindle abundance in its upper third, at 34.71% of muscle length. The source recommends the radial region as the priority target for this muscle. This atlas splits flexor digitorum profundus into an index compartment and a middle/ring/little compartment, while the source splits it into a radial half (anterior interosseous nerve) and an ulnar half (ulnar nerve). Those two divisions do not coincide: the middle/ring/little compartment straddles both halves, so it carries both of the source's regions, while the index compartment carries only the radial one.
motor_endplate_zones.source: Zhou J, Jia F, Chen P, Zhou G, Wang M, Wu J, Yang S, 'Localisation of the centre of the highest region of muscle spindle abundance of anterior forearm muscles', J Anat 244(5):803-814 (2023), doi:10.1111/joa.14000 -- 24 adult cadavers, modified Sihler's staining with muscle-spindle histology and spiral CT localisation

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Transverse on the volar forearm at roughly half its length.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Deep layer of the anterior compartment, lying directly on the radial and ulnar cortices, deep to flexor digitorum superficialis.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: Four bellies for digits II-V. The thumb is NOT included -- its distal phalanx is flexed by flexor pollicis longus, a separate muscle -- so targeting 'FDP' always means FDP2-5.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Diaconu S et al. (Elias University Hospital), 'A Visual Guide to Ultrasound-Guided Botulinum Toxin Injection in Spasticity: Part I -- Distal Upper Limb Muscles', Toxins 17(3):107 (2025), doi:10.3390/toxins17030107

trigger_points.location_description: Deep bellies in the middle third of the forearm, palpated through flexor digitorum superficialis or along the ulnar border between flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulna.
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Same digital pattern as flexor digitorum superficialis (palmar aspect of the corresponding finger to the fingertip); Travell and Simons do not separate the two clinically.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: As for flexor digitorum superficialis: prolonged or forceful gripping (tools, steering, climbing), sudden overload.
trigger_points.notes: The source document states activation/perpetuation and referral pattern for FDP are as for FDS, since Travell and Simons do not distinguish a separate FDP referral pattern.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons (1999) Trigger Point Manual, 2nd ed., Vol. 1, ch. 38; Donnelly et al. (2019) 3rd ed., ch. 38 -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded wrist muscle reference.

(2021) for attachments, innervation (root values as given by Gray's) and vascular supply; Travell, Simons & Simons' Trigger Point Manual, 2nd ed. (1999, Vol. 1) and 3rd ed. (2019) for trigger-point (TrP) locations and referred-pain patterns; Green's Operative Hand Surgery 8th ed. (2022) [4], Neumann (2017) [5], Kendall (2005) [6] and Kapandji (2019) [7] for kinesiology, Netter (2023) [54] for topographic cross-checking; and peer-reviewed primary literature for biomechanics, variants and clinical entities. Bracketed numbers point to the master list in Appendix B; every profile ends with its own reference list. Claims that could not be tied to a verified source are labelled [clinical reasoning] or [UNVERIFIED]. Appendix A grades the match between each key claim and its source.
clinical.function_biomechanics: Major: Flexion of the DIP joints (the only DIP flexor), then PIP and MCP flexion; hook and power grip [1, 5]. At the wrist: Secondary wrist flexor; with the fingers extended it contributes a flexion moment at the wrist and limits combined wrist and finger extension (basis of extrinsic tightness testing) [5]. Together with FDS it dominates flexor-side PCSA [9]. Quadriga: Because the middle, ring and little tendons share one belly, shortening or tethering of one tendon limits excursion and flexion power of the neighbours [4]. Importance: Recipient of ECRL in spastic and tetraplegic hands (Boyes) and of FDS in FDS-to-FDP transfers; the muscle most affected in Volkmann's ischaemic contracture [4].
clinical.adjacent_structures: Bursae / sheaths: Ulnar bursa; digital flexor sheaths [1]. Relations: The anterior interosseous nerve and artery run on the interosseous membrane between FDP (ulnar) and FPL (radial); the ulnar nerve and artery lie on the anterior surface of FDP deep to FCU [1]. Coupled structures: Anterior interosseous nerve, median nerve in the carpal tunnel, lumbricals, digital pulleys, interosseous membrane (deep flexor compartment) [1, 4].

trigger_points.location: Deep bellies in the middle third of the forearm, palpated through FDS or along the ulnar border between FCU and the ulna [2, 3].
trigger_points.referred_pain: Same digital pattern as FDS (palmar finger to the tip); Travell and Simons do not separate the two clinically [2, 3].

clinical.notes: Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome (Kiloh–Nevin) weakens FPL, the FDP of the index and middle fingers and pronator quadratus, producing the inability to form a rounded "OK" sign [43]. Avulsion of the FDP insertion (jersey finger) is commonest in the ring finger; deep flexor compartment ischaemia produces Volkmann's contracture; ulnar-innervated FDP with intrinsic paralysis contributes to ulnar clawing [4].
clinical.caveat: Referred-pain maps from Travell and Simons are clinical consensus drawings, not experimentally derived; the APL and pronator quadratus maps (Hwang et al.) are experimental hypertonic-saline studies in healthy volunteers. Grade C items (Appendix A rows 23, 44–46, 48): TrP distances, muscle-level arterial detail, the ECRL/ECRB insertional bursa, the grip-strength claim for PL agenesis, and the extrapolated EDM/EPB/EPL referral statements. All are labelled in the text. Referred-pain conventions. "TrP referral" is the essential (dark) zone described by Travell and Simons unless "spillover" is stated. TrP locations in centimetres are approximations read from the Manual's figures and should be confirmed by palpation of the taut band. Quantitative biomechanical values are cadaveric means and vary with forearm rotation and wrist angle.
